passage: Transcript: A codex is not a stack of leaves. It is a set of gatherings — quires — each one made by folding sheets of parchment together and sewing through the fold, and if you want to know how a book was made, that is the unit you have to work in. Take the Sarnesfield Psalter. Most of its quires are of eight leaves; quires six and eleven have ten. Don't take my word for the count — go to the reading room and look at the thread. Now, before he wrote, this scribe pricked his leaves to guide the ruling. In this book he pricked them a gathering at a time — the holes run through all four sheets of a quire together — and you find them in the outer margin only, never the inner. Two hands copied this book. The second takes over at folio forty-seven, which falls in the middle of a quire, not at the start of one. And that is the constraint, because a scribe handed a gathering of his own would have begun at its first leaf. Vandeleur points out that quires six and eleven are also the two that carry no catchword at the foot, and takes the pair of anomalies to show that both were enlarged later to take in an added text. The pairing is real. What made it, I don't think we can say.
prompt: [Academic Talk — Codicology] How does the professor organise the talk?
choices: He raises a disagreement about one book, and then assembles the evidence that bears on it
He settles what the unit of evidence is, and then reads one book's features from it
He works through one book from the outside in, from its binding to its written page
He sets out two rival ways of reading a book's make-up, and then tests them on one
correct_answer: He settles what the unit of evidence is, and then reads one book's features from it
explanation: The first four sentences do one job, fixing the gathering as "the unit you have to work in", and everything after them is a feature of the Sarnesfield Psalter read off that unit: the leaf counts, the pricking, the point where the second hand takes over, and finally the two quires Vandeleur disputes; the disagreement arrives last rather than first, the binding is never a stage of the tour, and no second way of reading a book is ever put up against the quire.

distractor_rationales.choice: He raises a disagreement about one book, and then assembles the evidence that bears on it
distractor_rationales.reason: The disagreement with Vandeleur does arrive, but it arrives last; putting it first would make the whole talk a response to him, when the quire, the pricking and the change of hand are all established before his name is spoken.

distractor_rationales.choice: He works through one book from the outside in, from its binding to its written page
distractor_rationales.reason: The talk does move across the book, but not in that direction: it opens with the gathering, and the binding is never treated as a stage of its own.

distractor_rationales.choice: He sets out two rival ways of reading a book's make-up, and then tests them on one
distractor_rationales.reason: The gridiron-and-alloy shape of two competing methods is not what this talk has; the quire is offered as the unit to work in, not as one candidate unit among two.

prompt: [Academic Talk — Codicology] According to the professor, how were the leaves of this manuscript pricked?
choices: One sheet at a time, with the holes in both margins, inner as well as outer
A gathering at a time, with the holes in the outer margin only
A gathering at a time, with the holes in both margins, inner as well as outer
One sheet at a time, with the holes in the outer margin only
correct_answer: A gathering at a time, with the holes in the outer margin only
explanation: The professor gives both halves in one breath, that the scribe "pricked them a gathering at a time" so that "the holes run through all four sheets of a quire together", and that they are found "in the outer margin only, never the inner"; each of the other three keeps one half and reverses the other.

distractor_rationales.choice: One sheet at a time, with the holes in both margins, inner as well as outer
distractor_rationales.reason: Reverses both halves of what the professor says: the prickings run through a whole quire, and they are in the outer margin only.

distractor_rationales.choice: A gathering at a time, with the holes in both margins, inner as well as outer
distractor_rationales.reason: Keeps the batch pricking but adds an inner-margin row the professor explicitly denies when he says the holes are never in the inner margin.

distractor_rationales.choice: One sheet at a time, with the holes in the outer margin only
distractor_rationales.reason: Keeps the margin right and loses the batch: it is what a listener who caught the outer margin but not the holes running through all four sheets of a quire would choose.

prompt: [Academic Talk — Codicology] What does the professor conclude from where the second hand takes over?
choices: That the two scribes were each given whole gatherings of their own to copy
That the second scribe was working from an exemplar different from the first's
That the two scribes were not dividing the gatherings between them
That the change of hand came after the gatherings had already been sewn together
correct_answer: That the two scribes were not dividing the gatherings between them
explanation: The second hand takes over at folio forty-seven, which the professor says "falls in the middle of a quire, not at the start of one", and his reason is that "a scribe handed a gathering of his own would have begun at its first leaf", so the mid-quire position is what rules out each man holding gatherings of his own; a different exemplar and a change of hand after sewing are compatible with the same folio but are never the conclusion he draws.

distractor_rationales.choice: That the two scribes were each given whole gatherings of their own to copy
distractor_rationales.reason: The conclusion the professor would have drawn had the hand changed at the first leaf of a quire; it is the exact reverse of what he says the mid-quire position rules out.

distractor_rationales.choice: That the second scribe was working from an exemplar different from the first's
distractor_rationales.reason: A real codicological inference from a mid-quire stint boundary, but one the professor does not draw; no exemplar is mentioned anywhere in the talk.

distractor_rationales.choice: That the change of hand came after the gatherings had already been sewn together
distractor_rationales.reason: Moves the conclusion from the order of work to the order of binding, which is the subject of the later dispute about quires six and eleven, not of this point. Nothing in the talk dates the sewing.

prompt: [Academic Talk — Codicology] Why does the professor say, 'go to the reading room and look at the thread'?
choices: To put his count of the leaves in the gatherings where a student can check it rather than take his say-so
To put the parchment's identification as calf or sheep where a student can check it rather than take his say-so
To put the dating of the two hands where a student can check it rather than take his say-so
To put the order in which the gatherings were bound where a student can check it rather than take his say-so
correct_answer: To put his count of the leaves in the gatherings where a student can check it rather than take his say-so
explanation: The line falls immediately after "Most of its quires are of eight leaves; quires six and eleven have ten", and the thread is what those leaf counts are read from, so the invitation is to check that figure at its source; the dating of the hands, the order of binding and the animal the skin came from are each things a reader could examine the book for, but none of them is an assertion the professor has just made.

distractor_rationales.choice: To put the parchment's identification as calf or sheep where a student can check it rather than take his say-so
distractor_rationales.reason: A real thing a reader of the book could settle for herself, but the professor never says what animal the parchment came from, so there is no claim of his here to be checked.

distractor_rationales.choice: To put the dating of the two hands where a student can check it rather than take his say-so
distractor_rationales.reason: The two hands are named later in the talk and are never dated, and the thread carries no evidence of date; the remark attaches to the figures the professor has just given.

distractor_rationales.choice: To put the order in which the gatherings were bound where a student can check it rather than take his say-so
distractor_rationales.reason: The order of the gatherings is the one thing the professor never puts in doubt; the sewing is offered as the evidence for how many leaves each gathering holds.

prompt: [Academic Talk — Codicology] What is the professor's response to Vandeleur?
choices: That the catchwords are indeed absent there, though their absence is common in books of this date
That an added text was indeed taken in, though it is unsettled when the book received it
That the two anomalies do fall on the same two quires, though what produced them is unsettled
That the two quires were indeed enlarged, though it is unsettled what they were enlarged for
correct_answer: That the two anomalies do fall on the same two quires, though what produced them is unsettled
explanation: The professor grants exactly the coincidence Vandeleur builds on — "The pairing is real" — and refuses only the explanation laid over it, saying of what made the pairing that "I don't think we can say"; the other three keep Vandeleur's conclusion in some form or dispute the leaf count, which the professor stated himself and never questions.

distractor_rationales.choice: That the catchwords are indeed absent there, though their absence is common in books of this date
distractor_rationales.reason: Grants the right half of the pairing but explains it away with a claim about other books that the professor never makes; he questions what caused the pairing, not how rare it is.

distractor_rationales.choice: That an added text was indeed taken in, though it is unsettled when the book received it
distractor_rationales.reason: Concedes the added text, which is the part of Vandeleur's reading the professor will not grant; he grants the pairing of anomalies and nothing beyond it.

distractor_rationales.choice: That the two quires were indeed enlarged, though it is unsettled what they were enlarged for
distractor_rationales.reason: Grants that an enlargement took place, which is precisely what the professor leaves open when he says of the pairing that he does not think we can say what made it.
